messages.subject: naiive occupancy by year
parts:
Hi everyone,

I was wondering if anyone had some code to calculate yearly naiive occupancy rates (colext). I currently use the following code provided by Jeffery Royle to get the overall naiive occupancy, but can't figure out how to modify it for yearly. I have 9 primary sampling occasions each with 4 secondary sampling occasions.

(sum(apply(getY(TISA_UMF), 1, function(x)
  any(x > 0, na.rm = TRUE)))) /
  nrow(INP_TISA)

Thanks in advance!

PS: For those new to unmarked, getY is a function built into unmarked, TISA_UMF is the name of my unmarkedMultFrame, and INP_TISA is the name of my dataframe containing my detection histories (used as input for TISA_UMF). And TISA just stands for Tiger Salamander.

parts:
Hi John,

function detHist( ) in package AICcmodavg outputs information on data
and "naive" statistics for different occupancy models. For instance, if
you run the example code of the colext( ) help page, you could output
the values as:

##fm is the model object in the example at bottom of ?colext
library(AICcmodavg)
out <- detHist(fm)
str(out)
out$out.props

Best,

Marc

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] naiive occupancy by year
parts:
Hi John,

I took a look at your data and I noticed that the sites in consecutive
years are different. You seem to have alternated the sites sampled each
other year, but there are no sites in common during two consecutive
years. You need sites that are common during consecutive years to get a
"naive estimate" and also to estimate occupancy dynamics. In other
words, you can neither compute the number of sites that were occupied
in year 1 and that were unoccupied in year 2 (extinction), nor the
number of sites unoccupied in year 1 that were occupied in year 2
(colonization). This explains the NaN.

Your best bet might be to fit a single season model with a year effect
in unmarked or fit a similar model with a site random effect in a
Bayesian framework.

Hope this helps,

Marc

Hi John,

indeed, the dynamic multi-season occupancy model does not assume closure. But in order to ESTIMATE the parameters that describe this lack of closure (= colonization and extinction/persistence rates), you need repeated measurements from the same sites. These parameters are transition rates and you can only estimate them when you can observe (some of) these transitions. Since you don't observe a single transition (all change is due to the change in the identity of the sampled sites), you can't estimate the parameters under the dynamic model and are restricted to inferences under a static multi-season model as Marc explains.

Best regards  ---- Marc

Hi John,

I took a look at your data and I noticed that the sites in consecutive
years are different. You seem to have alternated the sites sampled each
other year, but there are no sites in common during two consecutive
years. You need sites that are common during consecutive years to get a
"naive estimate" and also to estimate occupancy dynamics. In other
words, you can neither compute the number of sites that were occupied
in year 1 and that were unoccupied in year 2 (extinction), nor the
number of sites unoccupied in year 1 that were occupied in year 2
(colonization). This explains the NaN.

Your best bet might be to fit a single season model with a year effect
in unmarked or fit a similar model with a site random effect in a
Bayesian framework.

Couldn't resist curiosity (or at least a brief exploration). Yeah, I think it's reasonable to be extremely cautious when fitting dynamic models where no transitions are even partially observed. The likelihood is definitely multi-modal (there is a possible trajectory that is extremely dynamic, and a possible trajectory that is not very dynamic). Red bars in the graphic indicate estimates produced when every site is sampled each year, blue when every site is sampled every other year. Sloppy script below for anybody interested in digging deeper--I didn't mess around with optimizer settings. Sampling from the posterior seems likely to catch this, but I don't know what you do with two plausible alternatives: maybe more effective to look at trends in psi.





nsites<-400
nprimary<-10
nsec<-3
p<-0.4
nsims<-100

psi<-0.7

gam<-0.3
eps<-0.2
#b0.eps<--1
#b1.eps<-0.1
#b0.gam<--0.9
#b1.gam<-0.15

cov<-matrix(rnorm(nsites*nsims, 0, .5), nsites, nsims)

z<-array(NA, dim=c(nsites, nprimary, nsims))
library(boot)
for (s in 1:nsims){
for (i in 1:nsites){
  z[i, 1, s]<-rbinom(1, 1, psi)
  for (t in 2:nprimary){
    z[i, t, s]<-rbinom(1, 1, (z[i, t-1, s]*(1-eps)+(1-z[i, t-1, s])*gam))
  }
  }
}
y<-array(NA, dim=c(nsites, nprimary*nsec, nsims))

for (s in 1:nsims){
for (i in 1:nsites){
  for (t in 1:(nsec*nprimary)){
    y[i, t, s]<-rbinom(1,1, z[i, (floor((t-1)/nsec)+1), s]*p)
  }
  }
}

ysub<-y
ysub[, c(4:6, 10:12, 16:18, 22:24, 28:30),]<-NA

library(unmarked)

coefmatFull<-matrix(NA, nsims, 4)
coefmatRed<-matrix(NA, nsims, 4)

for (i in 1:nsims){
umf_1<-unmarkedMultFrame(y[,,i], siteCovs = NULL, obsCovs = NULL, numPrimary = nprimary)
umf_2<-unmarkedMultFrame(ysub[,,i], siteCovs = NULL, obsCovs = NULL, numPrimary = nprimary)
fit1<-colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf_1)
fit2<-colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf_2)
coefmatFull[i, ]<-coef(fit1)
coefmatRed[i, ]<-coef(fit2)
}


library(boot)
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
hist(inv.logit(coefmatFull[,2]), col=rgb(1,0,0,.5), main='', xlab=expression(hat(gamma)))
abline(v=0.3, lwd=3)

hist(inv.logit(coefmatFull[,3]), col=rgb(1,0,0,.5), main='', xlab=expression(hat(epsilon)))
abline(v=0.2, lwd=3)

hist(inv.logit(coefmatRed[,2]), col=rgb(0,0,1, .5),  main='', xlab=expression(hat(gamma)))
abline(v=0.3, lwd=3)

hist(inv.logit(coefmatRed[,3]), col=rgb(0,0,1, .5), main='', xlab=expression(hat(epsilon)))
abline(v=0.2, lwd=3)

    z[i, t, s]<-rbinom(1, 1, (z[i, t-1, s]*(1-eps)+(1-z[i, t-1, s])*gam))

  }

  }

}

y<-array(NA, dim=c(nsites, nprimary*nsec, nsims))

 

for (s in 1:nsims){

for (i in 1:nsites){

  for (t in 1:(nsec*nprimary)){

    y[i, t, s]<-rbinom(1,1, z[i, (floor((t-1)/nsec)+1), s]*p)

  }

  }

}

 

ysub<-y

ysub[, c(4:6, 10:12, 16:18, 22:24, 28:30),]<-NA

 

library(unmarked)

 

coefmatFull<-matrix(NA, nsims, 4)

coefmatRed<-matrix(NA, nsims, 4)

 

for (i in 1:nsims){

umf_1<-unmarkedMultFrame(y[,,i], siteCovs = NULL, obsCovs = NULL, numPrimary = nprimary)

umf_2<-unmarkedMultFrame(ysub[,,i], siteCovs = NULL, obsCovs = NULL, numPrimary = nprimary)

fit1<-colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf_1)

fit2<-colext(~1, ~1, ~1, ~1, umf_2)

coefmatFull[i, ]<-coef(fit1)

coefmatRed[i, ]<-coef(fit2)

}

 

 

library(boot)

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

hist(inv.logit(coefmatFull[,2]), col=rgb(1,0,0,.5), main='', xlab=expression(hat(gamma)))

abline(v=0.3, lwd=3)

abline(v=0.2, lwd=3)

 

hist(inv.logit(coefmatRed[,2]), col=rgb(0,0,1, .5),  main='', xlab=expression(hat(gamma)))

abline(v=0.3, lwd=3)

parts:
Hi Marc,

It looks like the situation is unchanged (maybe worse in this small set of realizations) if, say, half of the sites are surveyed on even years and half on odd years (I think this is kind of the sampling design John Vanek had?). One other artifact (not depicted here), if the number of sites shrinks (say to 200 or 100 vs. 400), the estimate for initial psi seems sit on the upper boundary somewhat regularly. I think that maybe John had referred to that issue in a previous thread, so this might be a reason.

There might be some sort of 'magic covariate' solution to this, although a single cov that increases colonization and decreases extinction leads to the same issue, as does two separate (site)covs weakly influencing each dynamic (below). I'd guess that this depends upon the overall trajectory (where the pr of one dynamic greatly exceeds another, seems like estimates would be more reasonable). 




There's a lot of parameter space/model space that could be explored, so John's data/fits could be perfectly fine. Seems like the easiest general solution is to model dynamics at a temporal scale that aligns with the sampling. I'm pretty sure I've seen this done (revisits of Joseph Grinnell's surveys in California, where state transitions reflect changes over 80 years?). With a staggered/every other year design, this might require some mishmashing of yearly covariates or yearly site covariates, but from an interpretation/inference standpoint, I don't know that you are losing too much.

All,

With budget cuts looming for many long-term studies one might see more of this kind of staggered/rotation design in that only a subset of potential sites can be surveyed in a single year.  Or even more likely, studies that started out with all sites surveyed every year suddenly having to switch to every other year because of budget cuts.  Although we don't use colext for the Marbled Murrelet at-sea surveys in the Pacific Northwest, we've had to switch to every-other-year surveying for each half of the surveyed areas because of drops in funding.

Jim Baldwin
